doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Arranging, bandleading and Pearl Bailey's life
title: His band's all-stars and Blue Mitchell, the underrated trumpeter
summary: He lists the band's players, praises Blue Mitchell as an unmarketed unsung hero, contrasts that with Pearl's publicists, and mentions the Blue and Shew record.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: It sounded like you had quite a lineup. You had some of the top players. You had Cat Anderson, Conte Candoli, Bobby Shew, Don Menza, Pete Christlieb, Ted Nash, Joe Romano, John Heard, George Duvivier – I guess they traded off on bass – Frank Strazzeri. Anybody they left out here in the dictionary?
And Blue Mitchell.
Oh yeah, Blue Mitchell. Great.

Bobby Shew would not play any jazz as long as Blue was in the band. He loved Blue Mitchell. Then when Blue Mitchell passed away, then Bobby started playing jazz too. But he loved Blue so much. He said, “As long as Blue’s here, he’s the boss.” Blue Mitchell was great, a great performer, a great guy.
What else can you say about Blue, since he’s overshadowed in the history of jazz, and here you had a really . . .?
An underrated player. He was not marketed. We tried to give him as much publicity as possible. But he’s one of the unsung heroes as far as trumpet players are concerned.
So why was it? Was it a personality situation? Or . . .?

I don’t know. Some of those things I don’t understand. Here’s some trumpet players that couldn’t even shine his shoes, and they get all the glory. I guess it’s up to who they have to market them. Half of those guys didn’t have a personal manager or a – what do you call them? Pearl had it. Pearl had a spokeman for her. What do they call it?
Publicist.
Publicist, yeah. I’m a little slow this morning.
Who was Pearl’s publicist and manager? Probably several different managers and publicists?
Yeah, she had several. Stan Irwin was her manager for a long time.
Say again?
Stan Irwin.
Irwin? Stan Irwin?

Yeah. Stan Irwin was responsible for getting Louis Prima and Keely Smith to the Sahara and negotiating that. That became big. Stan, he does things for me today. The publicist – she had several of them. They did a good job of keeping her in the foreground all the time, in front of the public eye, which is very important. People like Blue never had that. He was content with just blowing his horn. But thank God his name is emerging more.
Was he a quiet guy? Was he flamboyant? What was his personality like, Blue Mitchell?

He was a very happy guy, but he never pushed himself. He was low-key when it came to that. You said, “Blue, that was great.” He said, “Naw, that was nothing. I wasn’t on that day.” We made a record with Blue and Shew. You know about that record?
Uh-uh.
It’s a part of an album. That was the one where Bobby got the chance to play jazz along with Blue Mitchell. Bill Holman did the chart. It’s called Blue and Shew.
Did you play on that one too?
Yeah.
